headline: Parliament Passes Game-Herds Bill as India Trade Deal Advances Amid Sharp Disputes
summary: Parliament passed legislation allowing designated game-animal herds to be managed in national parks, despite opposition warnings about biodiversity and the lawmaking process. MPs also advanced the New Zealand–India free-trade agreement, which drew support from National, ACT and Labour but opposition from the Greens, New Zealand First and Te Pāti Māori over migration provisions, investment obligations and Māori participation. Question time featured disputes over workplace-safety reform, apprenticeship numbers and an education contract, while the House advanced a long-running Nelson land case and passed a redress bill for abuse in care.

topicSummaries.topic: Health and Safety Reform Sparks Coalition Dispute Over Workplace Risks
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes could affect how employers manage workplace hazards, with critics warning of greater risks to workers and the Minister arguing they will focus effort on the most serious dangers.
topicSummaries.content: Labour and Green MPs challenged Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden over a bill that would direct businesses to prioritise critical risks and reduce compliance requirements for lower-level hazards. Critics cited warnings from ACC and concerns raised by Pike River families, while van Velden said the reforms would strengthen practical protections and rejected the need for changes. New Zealand First leader Winston Peters questioned how the rules would apply to large and small contractors on the same worksite, and clashed with van Velden over whether he had sought a meeting about possible amendments. The bill remained under debate; no vote was recorded on it during the sitting.

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: I won’t be making changes, because my health and safety reforms focus on practical, common-sense changes that set businesses up for success in keeping people safe.

keyExchanges.speaker: Teanau Tuiono (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: What changes, if any, will she make to her health and safety reforms to address warnings from officials of “a real and material risk of increasing deaths, injuries, claims and costs”?

topicSummaries.topic: India FTA Passes First Reading Amid Disputes Over Migration and Māori Input
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: If implemented, the agreement will lower tariffs on New Zealand exports to India, while its investment, worker-mobility and consultation provisions remain subjects of political scrutiny.
topicSummaries.content: The India Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill passed its first reading 93–29 and was referred to the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee. Trade Minister Todd McClay said the agreement would reduce or remove tariffs on 95 percent of current exports to India, with 57 percent duty-free from day one and 82 percent when fully implemented; core dairy products were excluded. Labour supported sending the bill to committee but flagged uncertainty over a US$20 billion investment effort commitment and possible tariff clawbacks after 15 years. Winston Peters alleged that immigration settings were being tightened specifically for Indian nationals, risking damage to trade and diplomatic ties. Te Pāti Māori opposed the deal, saying Māori were excluded from co-design, while the Greens cited concerns about the agreement’s economic benefits, environmental and labour protections, and the time allowed for scrutiny.

keyExchanges.speaker: Todd McClay (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Ninety-five percent of tariffs will be eliminated or reduced at 57 percent duty-free from day one, rising to 82 percent of everything we sell being tariff-free when the agreement is fully enforced.

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (NZ First)
keyExchanges.quote: This is, after all, a trade agreement, not a migration pact, but National and ACT felt otherwise.

topicSummaries.topic: Game-Herds Bill Passes Despite Conservation and Biodiversity Warnings
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law changes how designated game-animal herds can be managed in national parks, balancing hunting access against the protection of native ecosystems.
topicSummaries.content: The Game Animal Council (Herds of Special Interest) Amendment Bill passed its third reading by 67 votes to 55. Hunting and Fishing Minister James Meager said designated herds would be managed through plans intended to control animal numbers while allowing hunting and conservation activity. Labour and Green MPs argued that allowing herds to remain in national parks could harm native plants and wildlife, and said the bill lacked adequate evidence, monitoring requirements and safeguards. Government supporters said the measure would apply in specific areas and include management plans and consultation with agencies. Labour also criticised the policy process and said its proposed amendments on monitoring, review and ecological measures had been rejected.

keyExchanges.speaker: James Meager (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Instead, a sensible, adaptive, management-focused herd management plan will manage those animals down to a level which achieves acceptable environmental and hunting outcomes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Brooking (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: It creates a legal pathway to deliberately maintain introduced species, such as deer, inside national parks for hunting purposes.

topicSummaries.topic: Minister Says Conservation-Land Disposal Clauses May Be Removed
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed change addresses public concern about whether conservation land could be sold, exchanged or developed, but the bill’s wording and final provisions remain unsettled.
topicSummaries.content: In response to questions about the Conservation Amendment Bill, Chris Penk, speaking for the Conservation Minister, said the Minister would recommend removing clauses concerning the disposal or exchange of conservation land. Penk said the bill had not created a realistic prospect of large-scale disposal and pointed to statutory tests, including consideration of threatened species, ecosystems and cultural and historical factors. On separate provisions allowing activities on conservation land, he said the wording was still being discussed with stakeholders and that strong environmental outcomes would remain a priority. No final amendments were confirmed in the exchange.

keyExchanges.speaker: Oriini Kaipara (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he stand by his statement, “There’s no way we’re going to sell off large swathes or large parcels of land in the conservation estate. We’re not going to do that”; if so, why is he proposing a bill that could make up to 60 percent of the conservation estate eligible for disposal, exchange, or development?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Penk (National), speaking for the Conservation Minister
keyExchanges.quote: He has advised stakeholders recently that he will consider, or rather that he will recommend to fellow Ministers the removal of the particular clauses in relation to the disposal or exchange of conservation land within the bill.

topicSummaries.topic: Apprentice Enrolments Fall to 35,825, Down From 47,475
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The decline signals fewer learners entering apprenticeship programmes, affecting access to skilled trades and the future workforce.
topicSummaries.content: Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds said 35,825 learners were enrolled in apprenticeships on 31 May 2026, compared with 47,475 at the closest available date in November 2023. She attributed the fall to lower business confidence, higher costs and economic pressure, particularly in construction. Labour questioned the Government’s apprenticeship funding and the reprioritisation of $3 million in underspent Apprenticeship Boost money; Simmonds said the programme had been extended and targeted at areas with skill shortages, and that the money was redirected to industry skills boards to improve retention and completion. She said apprenticeship completion rates had risen from 67 percent in 2021 to 86 percent.

keyExchanges.speaker: Shanan Halbert (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How many apprentices were there on 27 November 2023, and how many are there today?

keyExchanges.speaker: Penny Simmonds (National)
keyExchanges.quote: There were 47,475 learners enrolled in an apprenticeship programme; and on 31 May 2026, which, again, is as close to this date as I can get, there are 35,825 learners enrolled in an apprenticeship programme.

topicSummaries.topic: Education Minister Corrects Account of Learning First Email
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The correction adds to questions about how an overseas company was engaged for curriculum benchmarking while a New Zealand provider said it could have bid.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ginny Andersen questioned Education Minister Erica Stanford about a direct contract awarded to Australian firm Learning First for curriculum benchmarking, including whether the Minister knew a political adviser had discussed the work with the company’s chief executive. Stanford initially said she thought she first became aware of that particular exchange through an Official Information Act release. Later in the sitting, she corrected her answer, saying an email chain referred to by Andersen had been forwarded to her on 11 August 2024. Stanford said the Ministry of Education and the Education Review Office had introduced her to the company’s chief executive; she said the ministry’s later contracting decision was not a matter for her.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Was she or was she not aware that her adviser directly engaged with Ben Jensen, the chief executive of Learning First, specifically about the benchmarking of the New Zealand Curriculum before a contract was exclusively signed with them?

keyExchanges.speaker: Erica Stanford (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I’ve since gone back and reviewed all my records to make absolutely sure, and I’ve identified that there was an email chain to which the member referred to forwarded to me on 11 August 2024.

topicSummaries.topic: Nelson Tenths Bill Advances to Committee After Cross-Party Support
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill provides for legal title to trust land to be transferred to trustees representing descendants of customary owners after a long-running court case over an 1840s land promise.
topicSummaries.content: The Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, with a report due by 29 July. Attorney-General Chris Bishop said the bill would implement parts of a 2025 resolution agreement following litigation in which the High Court found the Crown had held land on trust for descendants of customary owners. The legislation provides for the transfer of legal title to the trust’s trustees and arrangements for continued public access and some ongoing government uses. Speakers from across parties supported the bill, while Te Pāti Māori described the case as a reminder of the Crown’s failure to honour its commitments. The bill is a private-law matter, rather than a Treaty settlement.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The primary purpose of the bill is to provide for the transfer of legal title to the trust land from the Crown to the new trustees of Te Here ā Nuku Trust.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willie Jackson (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: They could have asked for every acre back, but they’ve compromised and they’ve worked in a pragmatic way.

topicSummaries.topic: Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill Passes Third Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill advances a system intended to provide redress for people who experienced abuse while in care.
topicSummaries.content: The Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill passed its third reading by 67 votes to 55, with National, ACT and New Zealand First voting in favour and Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori voting against. The vote was formally recorded after Labour sought leave for a recorded division. The transcript provides no further debate on the bill during this sitting.

topicSummaries.topic: $93.5 Million Set Aside for Children With High Support Needs
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The four-year investment is intended to provide more stable placements and earlier clinical and care support for children and young people with complex needs.
topicSummaries.content: Children’s Minister Karen Chhour said Budget 2026 includes $93.5 million over four years for a range of care options, including specialist placements and clinical support. She said the funding is intended to prevent placement breakdowns and provide help earlier, and could address unmet needs that may otherwise escalate into more restrictive care. The announcement was made during oral questions; no further legislative decision was recorded.

topicSummaries.topic: Customs Reports 22 Arrests in Investigation Into Drug Couriers
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Customs says organised crime groups are recruiting young New Zealanders as couriers, exposing them to serious criminal penalties and risks overseas.
topicSummaries.content: Customs Minister Casey Costello told the House that six couriers and organisers linked to an organised crime syndicate had been arrested, bringing the wider investigation to 22 arrests and 31 search warrants since January. She said the syndicate was recruiting young New Zealanders to carry drugs and described joint work between government agencies, police and industry as important to disrupting the activity. Costello said more than $100 million had been invested over the previous two Budgets to support Customs and Police border-security work.

keyExchanges.speaker: Andy Foster (NZ First)
keyExchanges.quote: Why are these arrests so concerning?

keyExchanges.speaker: Casey Costello (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Organised crime groups are now actively recruiting young Kiwis to be drug couriers.

conclusion: The House advanced major trade and land measures, but the sitting exposed enduring disagreements over worker protections, environmental safeguards and whose interests are represented in national policy.
